title: Building Clinical AI Agents with LangGraph: Abridge's Eval Stack for High-Stakes Healthcare

segments.text: Hi everyone.
Thank you so much for being here. I'm
Janie. I'm the vice president of product
at Abridge and excited to chat about
shipping AI and agents in really
high-stakes and highly regulated
industries and share a little bit about
some of our journey.
So, just to give a little bit of context
about Abridge, we are a clinical
intelligence platform. We've started
solving and building tools for
clinicians, solving as many of their
clerical and clinical workflows as
possible, really starting at the
patient-clinician conversation. There
are over 2 billion conversations that
happen every single year in the US and
we think that the conversation is
probably one of the most important
workflows in health care.
It's obviously where patients and
clinicians and and doctors are giving
and receiving care, but if you think
about the 20% of our GDP that goes
towards health care, so much of it is
downstream or a derivative of that
conversation, whether it's the notes,
the billing codes, the claims, the prior
authorizations, the medications.
And where we're at today, the first
product that we built is we built the
infra, the product, and the customer
value to capture this conversation,
which has historically been fully
unstructured data, and to turn it into a
clinically useful chart or note for
doctors. And in a world today where um
there's a massive doctor shortage in the
country, especially post-COVID, and
doctors are burning out. They spend 10
to 20 hours after hours during what they
call pajama time on documentation. We've
done a really good job on delivering on
the ROI of saving time. And now that we
have all of this data, have gotten into
this wedge of the most important
workflow,
the new products that we've been
building are really to help us deliver
on our second and third acts, which are
how do we help health systems save and
make more money, and given clinicians
are opening our app before, during, and
after a patient walks in the room, how
might we actually save lives? And we say
that with all humility. So, with that,
um
we've scaled quickly. We're at 250 of
the largest health systems in the
country, the Mayos, the Kaisers, Johns
Hopkins of the world. And we've also put
ourselves in the center of healthcare's
data layer. The most important signal in
healthcare has historically, like I
said, been unstructured and uncaptured.
And because we now have this scale and
have all of this data, we've managed to
get all of these unparalleled data
network effects. We have over 100
million conversations that happen on our
platform on an annual basis.
With the data rights that we've received
explicitly from our customers, we're
able to de-identify it, and we're
learning constantly, whether it's edits
people are making to our notes, queries
people are asking with our Bridge AI
agent, and using that to improve our
models and continuously evaluate with
our LLM and human evaluations, and
continue to deploy better and better
products so that it compounds over time.
That's a little bit about the company,
and excited to actually get into the
content, which is what does it mean to
actually build AI and agents in these
high-stakes, high-trust environments?
There are a few things that shape all of
our product, business, and technical
decisions. I think the first one is the
bar for what we can ship is just
incredibly high, and so velocity can't
come at the expense of quality. The
reason for that is the stakes are quite
high. If we incorrectly label a
medication or a dosage, that has real
patient safety implications. And HIPAA
and the way that we use and take care of
PHI data have to shape every decision
that we make.
And finally, especially in enterprise
healthcare, buyers are choosing who
they'll even talk to based on security
and trust. Something that we like to say
internally is trust is earned in drops,
but lost in buckets. And so we know that
any single model release that has
massively negative implications could
lose the trust we have with customers.
We'll walk through two quick case
studies to show how we build and ship
quickly despite all of these things that
we're thinking about constantly. We'll
start first with our core notes product
and then move on to our agent system,
which is what we've built on top.
So the notes we create for doctors are
the core product. It's how we landed at
the scale that we did.
Basic high-level gist is
a doctor will open our app. They'll
record the conversation they have with a
patient with consent, and we'll turn
that into a clinically useful chart or
note that then gets submitted into the
electronic health record.
Notes are really hard. It's not just a
summary of a meeting or a conversation,
and the reason for that is the note that
we create ultimately becomes the bill,
the thing the hospital and the doctor
gets compensated for. So accuracy is
extremely important. And all of this
also becomes part of a patient's
longitudinal record, and quality matters
in ways that I think um a lot of ML
products don't experience. A few
examples, if we have misattribution in
our notes, so a note that might assign a
statement or a symptom or a decision to
the wrong uh person,
we have really, really large medical and
legally significant ramifications. For
example, a patient saying that they have
a symptom is very different than a
doctor explicitly diagnosing it and
billing for it. And if you're diagnosing
and billing the wrong things, there will
be a severe consequences for upcoding or
downcoding.
Similarly, confabulation or
hallucinations, if we are putting orders
for a medication that wasn't actually
prescribed or putting the wrong dosage,
huge huge patient safety issues.
As we've had some of these issues in
internal testing, the biggest pain in
trying to fix these was our release
process, namely getting the confidence
we needed to actually ship changes.
Prior to some of the changes we made a
while ago, releases would take us
anywhere from 1 to 2 months, and we had
clinicians annotating data, third-party
labels, labelers, and a lot of custom
tools that didn't talk to each other.
And we had a generic approach across the
platforms we chose, the actual ways in
which we hill climbed, and then finally
just good old human operational process
improvements. From a platform
perspective, we migrated to LangGraph.
We were using too many of our own
custom tools, and as we were scaling,
they weren't serving all of our use
cases. And LangGraph gave us unified
data sets, annotation, tracing,
evaluation in one system. And from an
enterprise security perspective, we were
allowed to self-host and also had the
access controls and auditability we
needed.
And we used LangSmith for our evals
platform. It gave us all the
customization we needed from a UI
perspective, and I think across
altitudes, whether it was debugging a
single encounter or seeing across all
all model releases, performance, we
could do it in one in
From an actual improvement perspective,
we
generally have the gift of a lot of
feedback given how important this
product is to clinician's workflows. And
across all of the clinician and user
feedback both in product and out of
product, we had a whole issue whole list
of model issues we knew we wanted to
improve. We would prioritize it by both
prevalence, so how often was it
happening, as well as the severity of
the issue. If we got it wrong, were the
stakes really high? And with that, we
organized all of these model issues into
an aggregate set of pillars. So, think
things like accuracy, compliance, style,
completeness.
And we started to go one by one and
create judges against these model
issues. Originally, it was pretty
cumbersome. We would have a clinician
who knew the subject matter well design
the annotation guide. We'd label the
encounters, and then someone would
actually iterate on prompts to get the
judge to match the clinician labels.
Really slow. We moved to an APO
framework, and it now takes the
annotation guide and the labeled
encounters and generates the calibrated
judge automatically to reduce turnaround
times.
The thing that always keeps me up at
night are just making sure that the
underlying data is actually correct and
high quality. This is the basis of
everything that we do.
A few things that are very helpful to
us, we make sure that the annotations
are actually matching the expected
outputs of our LLM judges.
We also like to collect free text
explanations from our annotators. Um
obviously, when there are issues or
inconsistencies, it allows us to debug.
But more importantly, um when things
aren't broken, we ask for it because it
allows us to check that the people who
are annotating and evaluating are
actually paying attention. And so, if
people are just clicking through, this
is a good way to really understand the
quality of our data.
And then finally, we always think about
what is the actual expertise we need up
front. There's certain evaluation or
data sets where we need a board
certified physician. Sometimes you might
need a specialist, but laying that up
very very explicitly has really helped.
Another design decision that's worth
calling out is how we use both
reference-free and reference-based
judges to make sure that we have a
blended approach instead of layers that
complement each other.
We have reference-free judges. They
generalize across all encounters and
they'll look at the note and the
conversation and score it and it doesn't
need a gold standard note to compare
against. And that means we can run them
offline, but more importantly online at
all times to continuously monitor the
quality of our notes.
They definitely have limits.
There's a lot of encounter-specific
nuance and specificity that gets met
and notes are just so inherently
subjective. So we supplement it with
reference-based judges that get as
specific as the specialty level and with
these two approaches, we're able to have
really high confidence in what we're
serving.
And even with these evals, I say that we
can't push to prod just because of the
stakes that we're operating in. Offline
evals happen first. They now happen very
very quickly with the process I just
described. They're really easy, but we
still will backtest against historical
encounters, also very quick. And I think
something that might be more unique to
the industry that we're operating in is
the way in which we do AB testing. When
I first joined a Bridge, I never thought
AB testing would be possible in
healthcare at this enterprise level.
Because we've earned the trust, we've
gotten explicit buy-in from a set of our
partners and customers who said, "Given
what you're doing upstream, I'm okay
with a silent release without knowing
about it, and we're willing to be, you
know, in your first 10 to 15% of
customers willing to innovate with you."
Definitely a privilege and a lot of
trust that we need to keep, but it
allows us to look again for more signal.
Are people editing the note? What are
the ratings they're leaving? Are we
getting really, really loud qualitative
feedback? And this is usually signal
we'll get instantly if it is so. And
that finally gives us the confidence to
actually go through a full release, and
we'll do our continuous online
monitoring.
Before this would take us 1 to 2 months,
and now we can get through this in days
and be at a place where where there's a
new model update, we feel really good
about getting the signal that we need.
And so, really exciting. We've seen
improvements over the past few quarters
in making sure that we can continue to
hill climb, and more importantly, our
users are telling us when we ship models
that they feel it instantly.
Now, I'll move on to the second case
study. Notes are the foundation of what
we do, and we've built on top a more
generic a bridge assistant. Um and
generally, we want to help clinicians
make the best decisions they can at the
right moment with the right context. But
the reality is most tools that
clinicians use today
fail on adoption and aren't really used.
There's a lot of constraints. First is
doctors are very busy. They're going
back-to-back 15-minute appointments.
They don't have the time to pull
something up, look up the context of a
patient. A lot of existing tools also
make them for make them choose between
security or no security. And with these
fragmented workflows, what we did was
build a unified agent that persists
across the workflows. So before the
visit, during that visit, after the
visit, there's a uniform UX and agent
that they could work with. And we
decided to fold a lot of separate
features and capabilities into one agent
that has really composable capabilities.
Examples are
capabilities like being able to search
patient context across multiple systems
of record or actually doing actions like
editing your note or placing a
medication or an MRI. And then finally
enabling something like clinical
decision support. So if a doctor has a
question,
can we support them via really searching
against literature that comes from
validated medical evidence.
And instead of these multiple features
living in disparate places, having it as
a singular agent allows us to call the
right tool at the right time, but also
deliver really coherent experience.
From more of a product perspective,
these are some of the principles that we
used in building this to make sure that
we weren't overwhelming our doctors and
clinicians.
The first is we like to say that we try
to be like air conditioning. We want to
be on in the background making things
better, but not have to actively be
present unless we think there's
something really important.
The second is agency. In healthcare
especially, it is really, really
important that clinicians know that
they're in control. We might be able to
suggest things, but ultimately we want
clinicians to use all the data at hand
and make the right decision.
The third is responsiveness.
This can come in a lot of different
forms. If a clinician is explicitly
giving us the gift of feedback, we want
to make sure that our products and
systems are actively listening and
improving quickly, but because of where
we operate, we also can implicitly learn
a lot to make the product better. So,
this might be if a clinician is
constantly making the same edits on a
note, can we learn their style to
automatically apply this to all future
notes?
Or, given the context that we have about
the patient the clinician is seeing, how
might we suggest through this agent
things that they might ask at certain
moments of the visit with their patient
to deliver better care?
And as we built this, I think similar
underlying machinery from an Evals
perspective, but the complexity went up
a magnitude just because we're not now
using single-step models. Some of the
eval criteria that we thought about,
clinical quality, is it actually
accurate?
Safety, are we making sure that this
agent isn't actively recommending things
that would harm the patient?
Boundary and adversary testing, what is
happening at the edges? Making sure that
the agent isn't answering questions
on things that isn't answering questions
that it wasn't trained to do. And
finally, from a tool selection
perspective, is the agent picking the
right tool and behaving the way that a
clinician would respond?
So, with that, I think the two takeaways
I hope to leave folks with is first,
you don't have to sacrifice on velocity
and or quality. I think if you invest in
the right eval infrastructure up front
and are really, really specific on the
things at which your product needs to
get right, you can do both quickly and
probably know the outputs of your
product even more deeply.
And second, maybe more on a personal
note, hopefully this has excited some
folks to potentially think about
building in healthcare. I think from an
impact perspective, healthcare is
probably where we need some of our best
builders, and there's probably no more
universal or important problem.
Given 20% of our GDP is going towards
here, I also think this is where the
largest businesses will get created. And
given the high stakes, I think some of
the hardest AI challenges will also need
to be solved here. So, um thank you so
much for your time. Enjoy the rest of
your day, and I'll be around.
>> [applause]
